introduction: On this third Sunday of Easter, Peter proclaims on Pentecost that God raised Jesus from the dead. In the Gospel, two disciples walking to Emmaus meet a stranger who explains the Scriptures to them; their hearts burn, and they recognize him in the breaking of the bread. Peter reminds us that we were redeemed by the precious blood of Christ. Let us recognize the risen Lord in his word and at this table.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the risen Lord walks with us and opens the Scriptures to us. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may help all who are discouraged to recognize the risen Christ walking beside them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who have lost hope: that the Lord may meet them on their road and set their hearts on fire. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who proclaim the Scriptures: that they may open them as Jesus did for the disciples at Emmaus. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are far from the Eucharist: that they may recognize Christ again in the breaking of the bread. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may say to Jesus, Stay with us. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, your risen Son walked with the disciples and was made known to them in the breaking of the bread. Open our hearts to his word, and stay with us always. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Stay with us
reflection.body:
On the afternoon of the first Easter, two disciples are walking home to Emmaus, sad and disappointed. A stranger joins them and asks what they are discussing. One of them, Cleopas, is astonished: "Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who doesn't know the things which have happened there in these days?" Then they tell him about Jesus and add one of the saddest lines in the Gospels: "But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel."

The stranger is Jesus, but "their eyes were kept from recognizing him." He tells them they have been slow to believe the prophets: "Didn't the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?" Then, "Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself."

When they reach the village, he seems to be going on. They invite him: "Stay with us, for it is almost evening." At table, "he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them. Their eyes were opened and they recognized him." Then he vanishes. And they say to each other, "Weren't our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?"

This story is the shape of every Mass. First Jesus speaks to us in the Scriptures; then he gives himself in the breaking of the bread. And like the two disciples, we are sent back to share the news.

Peter tells us the price of our redemption: not "silver or gold," but "precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ."

This week, if you feel like the disciples on the road, disappointed or confused, tell Jesus honestly. Read the Scriptures and ask him to open them to you. And at Mass, watch for him in the breaking of the bread.
